deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivation. It is a faint pencil draft, much of it struck through, of the historical and methodological introduction to Riemann's lectures on the partial differential equations of physics. The next page states the same programme in clean form: the true foundations of physical theories are partial differential equations. These are laws governing how quantities change from place to place in infinitely small regions, not hypotheses about hidden mechanisms.

Upper left column (heavily cancelled). The legible fragments ('Der Geist ...', '... die eigentliche ...', '... der Erfahrung ...') argue that the proper method of natural science rests on experience and on elementary laws. They do not rest on speculative assumptions.

Lower left column. 'Dasselbe gilt auch von den ... [Erscheinungen?] ... nur durch Annahmen [?] ... Erfahrung ...' extends this point to further classes of phenomena. Then comes a historical example: '... Laplace [?] im Jahre 1782 ... Untersuchungen ... Himmelskörper [?] ...'. The bottom line, running into the right column, reads roughly '... ein Gesetz ableitete, nach welchem [sich die Anziehungskraft?] von Ort zu Ort ändert'.

My own completion, not on the page: this is Laplace's 1782 work on the attraction of spheroids. There the gravitational potential V outside the attracting masses satisfies V_xx + V_yy + V_zz = 0. The next page begins 'diese partielle Differentialgleichung bildet die Grundlage ...', which confirms the reading. That page then gives terrestrial magnetism as a parallel case: the law of variation of the force from place to place is independent of how the magnetic particles are arranged inside the Earth.

Right column (very faint). The text continues the same rhetoric, with 'Erfahrung' recurring. No formulas are visible anywhere on the page.
errors: No mathematical content to check. One historical point: Laplace's equation for the potential is usually dated to his memoir on the attraction of spheroids (Théorie des attractions des sphéroïdes et de la figure des planètes, written 1782, published 1785). Riemann's date of 1782 matches this.
The reading 'Laplace' next to 'Jahre 1782' is uncertain because the pencil is extremely faint.

results.what: Historical remark that Laplace (1782), in studying the attraction of celestial bodies, derived the law by which the attractive force changes from place to place. This is a partial differential equation for the potential and serves as the model of a physical law.
results.modern_name: Laplace's equation for the Newtonian potential
results.usually_credited_to: P.-S. Laplace (1782/1785); Lagrange introduced the potential function in 1773

results.what: Methodological thesis that physical laws should be stated as laws in the infinitely small (PDEs), derived from experience rather than from hypotheses about hidden mechanisms.
results.modern_name: Field-theoretic / local formulation of physical law
results.usually_credited_to: General 19th-century view (Fourier, Faraday, Maxwell); Riemann's version is known from the introduction to his PDE lectures (Hattendorff ed.) and from his Naturphilosophie fragments

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a cancelled draft of the standard historical and methodological introduction to Riemann's lectures on the PDEs of physics. Its content (Laplace 1782, laws as PDEs) is already known from his published lectures and Naturphilosophie fragments. It contains no mathematics.

checkable.asserts: My addition, implied by context and not on the page: the Newtonian potential 1/r satisfies Laplace's equation away from the origin. This is the 'law from place to place' that Laplace derived in 1782.

transcription_corrections: Lower left: the line before 'Jahre 1782' appears to contain a name, plausibly 'Laplace' ('... Laplace im Jahre 1782 ...'). The following lines plausibly read '... Untersuchungen ... Himmelskörper ...'.

The bottom line, running across into the right half, reads roughly '... ein Gesetz ableitete, nach welchem ... von Ort zu Ort ...'. This links directly to the next page's 'diese partielle Differentialgleichung'.
Upper left block: almost all lines (rows 5-8 and 10 onward) are struck through, and the whole block is closed off by a diagonal cancellation stroke.
The archival folio number '195' is circled at the right margin.
